newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Moskow sees U.S. economy doing well in '97.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Moskow sees U.S. economy doing well in '97.

text.p: The U.S. economy did well in 1996 and should continue performing in a similar manner in 1997, Michael Moskow, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, said Thursday.
"The economy did well last year and we can expect more of the same in '97," Moskow said in text of a speech delivered to a business group here.

Moskow said he expected real U.S. gross domestic product will grow at between two- and 2-1/2 percent this year, the consumer price index should come in at about a three-percent rate, and the unemployment rate should fluctuate around 5-1/2 percent.

"We should have another year of respectable growth, with low inflation and low unemployment rates," he said. "In other words, a year that would be consistent with the Fed's goal of a healthy, growing economy with price stability."

Moskow said U.S. workers probably have not been more aggressive in seeking higher wages partly because of a "lingering sense of insecurity" in the workforce and said they seem more concerned about job security than wage increases.

"At some point, though, workers may begin feeling more secure and become more aggressive in seeking wage increases," he said. "We're watching carefully for any signs that wage pressures are mounting more than can be justified by productivity gains. We haven't seen that yet."
He expected consumer disposable income in 1997 to continue rising at a "healthy pace" that bodes well for spending.

Moskow noted also that although consumers have been using a "relatively high percentage" of disposable income to service their debt, the situation has been improving. He said the growth in consumer credit has slowed this year from the double-digit pace of 1994 and 1995, and debt service payments relative to income -- although still high -- have stabilized.
"Overall, we don't think consumer debt will be a major constraint on spending," he said.
Internationally, Moskow said the outlook was a "tough call," noting that he looked for a boost in U.S. exports when the economies of U.S. trading partners eventually pick up.

"But I don't think we can count on a strong rebound for exports in '97," Moskow said. "Our best guess right now is the international sector will have a neutral effect on the U.S. economy." ((DerivativesDesk(312)408-8750/E-mail:derivatives@reuters.com))
